title: The bridge
hook: stones float; the squirrel carries sand

segments.voice: Yesterday: the search, and Sampati, the wingless old vulture who could see Sita across the sea. Ask the old bird.

Hanuman has leapt the ocean, found Sita, given her the ring, and set Lanka on fire. Now he's back, and the whole army stands on India's southern shore looking at the problem. Hanuman can jump a hundred yojanas. A monkey army can't. Rama sits on the beach for three days, in Valmiki's telling, asking the ocean to let them pass. The ocean doesn't answer. So Rama, furious, picks up his bow and aims an arrow at the sea itself. And the ocean rises out of the water, in person, and says: don't dry me up. There's another way.
screen: `AN ARMY AT THE EDGE OF THE SEA.` → `THREE DAYS, NO ANSWER.` → `RAMA AIMS AT THE OCEAN.`

segments.voice: The ocean god tells Rama that one of his monkeys, Nala, is the son of the builder of the gods, and can build a bridge the sea will hold up. So the army goes to work. They tear up trees, boulders and whole rocky hilltops, carry them to the water, and Nala lays them in a line. The stones float. In Valmiki it takes five days to reach Lanka. People call it Rama Setu. Setu means bridge: Rama's bridge. In later tellings, the monkeys write Rama's name on each stone, and that's why they float. And then there's the squirrel. You won't find it in Valmiki; it comes from later tellings, especially popular in the south. While the monkeys haul boulders, a little squirrel runs down to the water, rolls in it, rolls in the sand up the beach, and runs back to shake the sand off between the stones. Over and over. A monkey laughs at it, or nearly steps on it. What are you doing, tiny thing? Rama picks the squirrel up and says its work matters: it's filling the gaps the big stones leave. And he strokes its back with three fingers. Look at the Indian palm squirrel: three pale stripes down its back. That, people say, is where Rama touched it. The story puts the two side by side. A giant project isn't only boulders. It's also the sand that keeps the boulders from wobbling. The big contributions are easy to see; the small ones hold them together. And whoever notices the squirrel is paying attention the way Rama does.
screen: `NALA, SON OF THE GODS' BUILDER.` · `THE STONES FLOAT: RAMA SETU.` · `A SQUIRREL CARRIES SAND.` · `THREE STRIPES WHERE RAMA TOUCHED IT.`

segments.voice: Think of something big you're part of, a family, a team, a school, a neighborhood, the work of looking after someone, and find your part in it that nobody sees: the dishes, the check-in text, the thing you fix without being asked. Don't measure it against the boulders; let the sand you've been carrying count. Then bring to mind someone else's small part you've never thanked.
Rama Setu. Rama's bridge: floating stones across the sea to Lanka, with a squirrel filling the gaps.
Your line: the squirrel counts. Sand is what keeps the stones still. Tomorrow, Ravana's court.

howItsDone: Rameswaram, on the Tamil Nadu coast, is an important pilgrimage place linked to the building of the bridge; the chain of shoals between India and Sri Lanka is often called Rama Setu, and the squirrel story is a favorite told to children.
